wine.name: Marqués de Riscal Rueda Verdejo
wine.grapes: Verdejo alone, by the house's technical sheets.
wine.sites: The house's own Verdejo vineyards on the stony Rueda plateau south of the Duero, farmed organically and certified so since 2018 by the house's account.
wine.making: Fermented at a controlled temperature in stainless steel, it stays on its fine lees in tank for one to two months, the lees stirred each week under nitrogen to keep air from a grape quick to brown, and it is bottled in the winter after the harvest, between January and March.
wine.glass: Fennel, aniseed and fresh cut grass with orange blossom and a hint of lime; smooth and fresh in the mouth, with a long finish and the faint bitter twist typical of Verdejo.
wine.ageing: Made to be drunk young, in the year or two after the vintage, while its fennel and grass are fresh.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass of medium size.

label.means: The Denominación de Origen of the plateau south of Valladolid, recognised on 12 January 1980, the first of Castilla y León.
On a Rueda label, a named grape makes at least 85 per cent of the wine; the house's sheets give Verdejo alone.
The Rioja house of 1858 at Elciego; its Rueda whites carry DO Rueda, never Rioja.

records.table: Marqués de Riscal Rueda Verdejo is the white of a Rioja house that turned to Rueda's own grape around 1970. Fermented in steel and kept briefly on its lees, it smells of fennel, aniseed and fresh grass: pour it cold and young.
records.story: Marqués de Riscal was founded in 1858 at Elciego in Rioja Alavesa, where in the 1860s, by the house's account, a master winemaker it hired brought in the methods of Bordeaux. A century later the house's consultant was the Bordeaux oenologist Émile Peynaud (1912 to 2004), and around 1970, by the denomination's own history, the house came to Rueda with him in search of a white of quality and found it in the local Verdejo, a grape quick to brown if it meets the air. In 1972, by the house's account, it made its first Rueda whites there, and in 1974 it brought Sauvignon Blanc to the district. It was among the bodegas that pressed for a Denominación de Origen, and Rueda was recognised on 12 January 1980, the first of Castilla y León. Since 2018 the house's own Rueda vineyards have been certified organic, by its account, and two of its Verdejos, Limousin and Finca Montico, carry the denomination's Gran Vino de Rueda mention. The Rueda Verdejo is the bottle a sommelier pours to show where modern Rueda began: Verdejo kept from the air, fresh, aromatic and young.

others.name: Marqués de Riscal Limousin
others.note: Verdejo from old vines on the high terraces of the Duero, fermented and aged on its lees in French oak and classified Gran Vino de Rueda.

others.name: Finca Montico

traps: Marqués de Riscal Rueda Verdejo carries DO Rueda, never Rioja: the house is a Rioja bodega of Elciego, but its whites grow in Castilla y León.
Rueda, recognised in 1980, is the first Denominación de Origen of Castilla y León, older than Ribera del Duero of 1982 and Toro of 1987.
A Rueda that names Verdejo needs at least 85 per cent of the grape, as one naming Sauvignon Blanc does; a white labelled simply Rueda needs only three quarters from the main white grapes together.

report: Searches for this record: 7 of the group's share of 35 (the house's history, sheets and Verdejo pages four times, the Consejo's history once, the Consejo's rules once, Peynaud's dates once); no fetch tried.

The plan's note on 1972: the house's history gives 1972 for its first Rueda whites and its Verdejo page a second bodega built in Rueda that year, one other house page says it expanded into Rueda in 1970, and the Consejo's history has it arrive around 1970 with Peynaud; the story keeps both, each hedged, and the region record's 1972 arrival is in tension with the Consejo's around 1970.

Peynaud's role rests on the Consejo's history with Spanish Wine Lover (spanishwinelover.com/marques-de-riscal-reinventing-a-rioja-icon) and JancisRobinson.com, which is not listed since its address names a writer; his dates, 29 June 1912 to 18 July 2004, are Wikipedia's and Decanter's, with Wine Spectator.

The 85 per cent rule and the green back label rest on the Consejo's page on its back labels (dorueda.com/los-vinos-de-la-d-o-rueda-mas-faciles-de-distinguir-con-sus-nuevas-contraetiquetas), which gives the orange label at a minimum of half Verdejo; the Gran Vino de Rueda mention (vines over thirty years, first vintage 2020) is on the Consejo's page of 2021.

The label today reads Marqués de Riscal Verdejo, marked 100 per cent organic, under DO Rueda; the record keeps the plan's words. The sheets read give Verdejo alone, so the library's note of Sauvignon Blanc in some bottlings is kept only as the library's.

Left out for want of a second source: Peynaud's teaching of the house's head in Bordeaux, his bringing the cool fermentation of Champagne to white Bordeaux (one source each), Sauvignon Blanc of 1974 as the district's first (the house's claim), the night harvest for this wine (the house's Sobre Lías Finas page says so for that wine only), vineyard areas and vine ages (volatile and in conflict) and the founder's name and dates (Guillermo Hurtado de Amézaga on the house's page, no dates found). Limousin's fermentation in barrel is the author's knowledge of the wine, on no page read, for the checker; the master winemaker of the 1860s is Jean Pineau on the house's page, his dates not found.
The house's sheet gives no serving temperature read; 8 to 10 degrees Celsius is the Codex's reference for a light, aromatic white served cold.
No swap proposed: the house's home is Rioja, which wave one teaches without it, and here it is the Rueda arm with a Rueda wine, as the plan intends. No living person met in the record.

wine.name: Belondrade y Lurton
wine.grapes: Verdejo, all or nearly all of it: the sheets of some vintages give a small share of other grapes beside it.
wine.sites: Quinta San Diego, the house's own estate at La Seca, a mosaic of some two dozen plots on different soils, slopes and aspects with vines of many ages, certified organic since 2010.
wine.making: Each plot is picked by hand and fermented apart with its own native yeasts in French oak barrels of several sizes, 300 and 500 litres among them, then aged on its lees for about ten months; the lots are chosen and blended, and the wine rests at least five months in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Fennel and lemon peel, with toast, fresh butter and praline from the lees and the barrel; creamy and full, held up by fresh acidity, with a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Open and generous in its first years, it is made, by the house's account, to be drunk over six to eight years, gaining depth in bottle.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius, as a full white; no need to decant, though a little air opens a young bottle; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The house's first and flagship wine, made since 1994, its name joining the founder's surname to Lurton.
The Denominación de Origen of the plateau south of Valladolid, recognised in 1980, the first of Castilla y León.

records.table: Belondrade y Lurton is the La Seca estate's Verdejo, fermented plot by plot with native yeasts in French oak and aged about ten months on its lees. Creamy and toasty, with fennel and lemon peel, it is a Rueda white for keeping: serve it as you would white Burgundy.
records.story: Belondrade began in 1994, when a Frenchman who had fallen for Verdejo set out to make a Rueda white for keeping, a single wine in the manner of a château, at a time when, by the house's account, a Verdejo made to age was a rarity in the district. He made the first Belondrade y Lurton that year in rented premises at Nava del Rey, and that first vintage reached the market in 1996. He bought vines at La Seca so that the wine would come wholly from his own estate, which he named Quinta San Diego after one of his children, and in 2000 the house opened its own cellar there. A rosé, Quinta Clarisa, named for his younger daughter, followed in 2000, and Quinta Apolonia, a younger Verdejo named for his elder daughter, in 2002. In 2005, by its own account, the cellar began to set commercial yeasts aside, and by 2010 it used none, the year the estate was certified organic. Every plot is fermented and aged apart in barrel, and the blend is chosen among the lots each year. Belondrade y Lurton shows a sommelier the other face of Verdejo: lees, oak and time in bottle rather than freshness alone.

report: Searches for this record: 8 of the group's share of 35 (five on the house's own domain, three wider); no fetch tried.

The plan's note is answered in part: 1994 is the house's year and that of Skurnik, Spanish Wine Lover and Berry Bros.; the first vintage made in 1994 at Nava del Rey and released in 1996, and the cellar at La Seca of 2000, rest on the house's history with Spanish Wine Lover; DO Rueda is on the house's sheet.

The plan's why calls the founders a French couple, one of them of the Lurton family of Bordeaux; only one source read (a search summary) said the founder was then married to a member of the Lurton family, and a second source read made her a cousin of two Lurton brothers already in Rueda, so the record says only that the name joins the founder's surname to Lurton, and the why should be checked.

Native yeasts from 2005 and none bought in by 2010, the organic certificate of 2010, the plots, the barrels of 300 and 500 litres, ten months on lees and five months at least in bottle rest on the house's own pages and sheets; the sheets give the plots as 22 and as 24, hence some two dozen, and the vines as 10 to 75 years old, left out as volatile.
The house's press dossier of 2024 says, through search, that from the 2018 vintage the wine came from two old plots, La Cruz and Alameda, alone; one reading only, so it is left out for the checker.

The glass rests on Spanish Wine Lover's tasting notes of the 2009, 2011 and 2012 vintages (fennel, lemon peel, fresh butter, praline, creamy); no serving temperature was read on the house's pages, so 10 to 13 degrees Celsius is the Codex's reference for a full white.

Left out: the claim, in one importer's account, that this was the first barrel fermented wine of Rueda; the founder's earlier career with an airline; the architect of the cellar; and the respelling, since no source gives the house's own pronunciation of the French surname.
Living names met, none in the fragment: the founder, his former wife of the Lurton name and his son and elder daughter as named by the sources; none of them is on people.json yet. No swap proposed.

wine.name: Termanthia
wine.grapes: Tinta de Toro alone, the local form of Tempranillo.
wine.sites: Ungrafted bush vines of Tinta de Toro more than a century old, rooted deep in sand and stones and never irrigated, in parcels the house keeps for Termanthia.
wine.making: The bunches are destemmed by hand and the fruit fermented in small French oak vats. The wine is aged around twenty months in French oak barrels, much of the wood new, with the share of new oak set vintage by vintage.
wine.glass: Inky purple; blackcurrant and cassis with violet, clove and nutmeg over black liquorice; full bodied and dense, with ripe, abundant tannin, warm alcohol and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Dense and marked by its oak when young, it wants several years in bottle and, by the house's account, can age for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour or two ahead; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The house's head wine, from ungrafted vines more than a century old, above Numanthia and Termes in its range.
The Denominación de Origen of the Duero around Toro in Zamora, recognised by an order of 29 May 1987.
The house at Valdefinjas, named for Numantia, the Celtiberian city that long held out against Rome.

records.table: Termanthia is Bodega Numanthia's head wine: Tinta de Toro from ungrafted vines more than a century old on Toro's sand, destemmed by hand and aged in French oak. Inky, dense and warm, with cassis, violet and liquorice, it wants a large glass and red meat.
records.story: The Denominación de Origen Toro was recognised by an order of 29 May 1987, on a stretch of the Duero whose sandy soils had kept phylloxera from spreading, so that old bush vines of Tinta de Toro stood there on their own roots. Numanthia was founded in 1998 by the Eguren family, growers from Rioja, with a cellar at Valdefinjas and old vineyards of the zone, among them ungrafted vines more than a century old. The family named the house after Numantia, the Celtiberian city that, as the house tells it, held off the Roman army for some twenty years, and it presents the name as a tribute to resilience, the same quality it sees in vines that came through phylloxera untouched. Three reds took shape: Termes, Numanthia and, from the ungrafted vines of more than a century, Termanthia. The wines drew notice abroad and helped put Toro on wine lists, and in 2008 the family sold the estate to the LVMH group. Termanthia is the bottle that teaches a sommelier why Toro's sand matters: vines old enough to give tiny crops of concentrated fruit, and a Toro red at full volume, ripe, inky and long in oak.

others.name: Numanthia
others.note: The house's middle red and its namesake, Tinta de Toro from old vines, aged about sixteen months in French oak.

others.name: Termes
others.note: The entry red of the house, also Tinta de Toro, aged in barrels with far less new oak.

traps: Termanthia is the head wine and Termes the entry, with Numanthia between them: the three names are easily swapped.
Tinta de Toro is Tempranillo under its local name, a form adapted to Toro's heat and sand, not a separate grape.
Toro's sand, not its altitude, is why phylloxera spared the old vines, which stand on their own roots.

questions.q: A guest asks why the vines behind Numanthia's Termanthia never needed grafting. Which answer fits?

The vineyards lie too high for the louse

questions.exp: Phylloxera spreads poorly through loose sand, so Toro's old bush vines stand on their own roots; altitude is not the reason, and Termanthia's vines are more than a century old.

report: Searches for this record: 6 of the group's share of 35 (three on the house's own domain, three wider); no fetch tried.

The plan's note is answered: Termanthia is taught as the head wine from the oldest ungrafted vines, Numanthia as the middle wine and Termes as the entry, as the library holds them; the founding family is named as a family and no living member is named.

The sale year is in conflict in the sources read: 2008 in the library, Winebid and the Wine Spectator and Decanter reports of the sale, 2005 in one account, the end of the 2006 vintage and the 2007 vintage in two more; the record keeps the library's 2008. Wine Spectator alone says the sale took in Termanthia's own small vineyard, left out; the DO's year of 1987 rests on the Consejo's copy of the order of 29 May 1987, cited in the Fariña record.

The making rests on the house's 2009 sheet (twenty months in new French oak barrels) and Decántalo (hand destemming, sorting and fermentation in French oak vats, twenty or twenty two months in barrel); one listing says the 2015 vintage began a smaller share of new oak, hence the share set vintage by vintage. The vines' age is about 120 years in Decántalo; the house speaks of ungrafted bush vines up to 200 years old and roots to five metres with no irrigation.

The glass follows the house's tasting note of the 2014 vintage (blackcurrant, cassis, violet, clove, nutmeg) with the library's ink and black liquorice; the house's page advises 14 to 15 degrees Celsius, and the record follows the Codex's service reference for a full red.

Left out for want of a second source: Termanthia's first vintage (none found), the name of its vineyard (Teso de los Carriles in one study aid only), the number of plots it now draws on, the founders' new project nearby after the sale and any score or price, which the tab refuses.

The region record's producers line speaks of cult prices, a judgement and a price this tab does not repeat. Living names met, none in the fragment: the Eguren winemaker of the founding years. No swap proposed.

wine.name: Pintia
wine.grapes: Tinta de Toro alone, the local form of Tempranillo.
wine.sites: Old vines of Tinta de Toro, many of them ungrafted, around San Román de Hornija and Pedrosa del Rey and towards Toro and Morales de Toro, on pebbly alluvial terraces of the Duero.
wine.making: Fermented in the house's cellar at San Román de Hornija, with the malolactic fermentation in wood, then aged about a year in barrels, mostly French oak with some American. From the 2020 vintage, by the house's sheet, amphorae joined the barrels for part of the ageing to soften the mark of the toast.
wine.glass: Cherry, black raspberry and prune with violet, liquorice and a toasty, smoky note from the barrel; powerful and dense yet juicy and silky, with fruity tannin and more freshness than its warmth suggests.
wine.ageing: Approachable within a few years of release, it keeps, by the house's account, for up to fifteen years in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, as the house advises; decant a young bottle an hour ahead; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The name of the house and of its one red, shared with a Vaccaean city on the Duero near Padilla de Duero.
The Denominación de Origen of the Duero around Toro, whose zone reaches into the province of Valladolid at San Román de Hornija.

records.table: Pintia is the Toro red the Álvarez family of Vega Sicilia created at San Román de Hornija: Tinta de Toro from old vines on the Duero's pebbly terraces, aged about a year in French and American oak. Ripe and juicy yet polished, it wants a decanter and a roast.
records.story: In April 1982 the Álvarez family bought Vega Sicilia in Ribera del Duero, and over the years that followed it built other wineries along the Duero and beyond, Alión in Ribera among them. Toro, downstream, had been a Denominación de Origen since 1987, a zone of Tinta de Toro whose sandy and pebbly ground had carried many old vines through phylloxera on their own roots. The family bought old vineyards there, many of them ungrafted, around San Román de Hornija, a village of the province of Valladolid that lies within the Toro zone, and built its cellar in the village. The first vintage sold under the name of Pintia was 2001. The wine's name is shared with Pintia, a city of the Vaccaei, a people of the Duero before Rome, whose remains lie near Padilla de Duero; the University of Valladolid's centre for Vaccaean studies has excavated the site, with the Vega Sicilia group among the centre's patrons. From the 2020 vintage, by the house's sheet, amphorae joined the barrels for part of the ageing, to soften the mark of toasted wood. Pintia shows a sommelier how the power of Tinta de Toro can be shaped in the cellar into a ripe, polished red.

report: Searches for this record: 7 of the group's share of 35 (three on the house's own domain, four wider); no fetch tried.

The plan's note is answered in part: the first vintage of 2001 rests on Spanish Wine Lover, Enterwine and Best of Wines, with a 2001 on Berry Bros. and Decanter; one account adds that the 1998, 1999 and 2000 were made as trials and one that the 2001 was first sold in 2004, single sources left out.

Founded is left empty: the idea of a Toro bodega is dated 1995 in one account, the purchase 1996 in another and the founding 1997 in a third, and one gives the present cellar as finished in 2006; the house's own pages read through search give no year.

The villages, the vine age of about 35 years, the barrels mostly French with some American, the malolactic in wood, the amphorae from 2020, 16 to 18 degrees Celsius and fifteen years of keeping rest on the house's sheets; the pebbly alluvial terraces on Enterwine and a merchant's listing, and many vines ungrafted on two secondary accounts.

The glass names fruit the sheets read did not: they speak of opulent, juicy, silky wine with sweet fruit and spicy wood, and the plum, black cherry and cocoa are the author's words for that, for the checker to try.

The Vaccaean city near Padilla de Duero and the Universidad de Valladolid's Centro de Estudios Vacceos rest on the centre's site and its papers in UVaDOC, which list Tempos Vega Sicilia among the centre's patrons; that the wine was named for the city rests on one account only, so the record says the name is shared.

The plan's note on Vega Sicilia is kept: wave one teaches Único in Ribera del Duero, and Pintia returns here as its own house with its own red; the others are named as the family's wines, not Pintia's, since the bodega makes one red.
Living names met, none in the fragment: the family's head and the winemaker of the early vintages (both on people.json) and the director of the excavations. No swap proposed.

changed: wine.glass: was ripe plum, black cherry and cocoa, the author's own words; now cherry, black raspberry and prune with violet, liquorice and a toasty, smoky note, powerful and dense yet juicy and silky, with fruity tannin and more freshness than its warmth suggests, on Berry Bros. for 2016, Bodeboca for 2014 and 2021 and the house's sheet for 2018.
open: Founded stays empty: Bodeboca gives the vineyards bought from 1997 to 2000 and the bodega founded in 2001, other accounts 1995, 1996 and 1997.
Many vines ungrafted rests on the author's two secondary accounts; the refuter's merchants give old vines of about 35 years, or 20 to 50, and say nothing of grafting.
The villages named in the sites rest on the house's sheet alone; no other page read names Pedrosa del Rey or Morales de Toro.

wine.name: Gran Colegiata Original
wine.classification: Reserva, an ageing category of the DO Toro
wine.grapes: Tinta de Toro alone, the local form of Tempranillo.
wine.sites: The house's ungrafted bush vines of Tinta de Toro, more than sixty years old by its sheet, picked by hand on the poor, sandy and pebbly ground of the Toro zone.
wine.making: Destemmed and fermented at 24 to 28 degrees Celsius for twelve to fifteen days, the wine is aged eighteen months in American oak barrels and then about three years in bottle before release, by the house's sheet.
wine.glass: Deep garnet; ripe blackberry and plum over cocoa, toast and vanilla from the American oak; full bodied and poised, with soft, silky tannin and a warm, long finish.
wine.ageing: Released ready to drink after its years in barrel and bottle, it holds and softens for several years more in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant an hour ahead and leave any sediment behind; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Named for the Colegiata de Santa María la Mayor, Toro's collegiate church begun in the twelfth century.
The house's nod to the first Gran Colegiata, whose Burgundy shaped bottle, by the house's account, it recalls.
In Toro, a red aged at least thirty six months, at least twelve of them in oak barrels.
The Denominación de Origen of the Duero around Toro, recognised by an order of 29 May 1987.

records.table: Gran Colegiata Original is Bodegas Fariña's classic Toro Reserva: Tinta de Toro from ungrafted vines of sixty years and more, eighteen months in American oak, then years in bottle. Liquorice, plum and vanilla over silky tannin; decant it and pour it with roast lamb.
records.story: Bodegas Fariña goes back to 1942, when, in the hard years after the Civil War, a couple from Porto de Sanabria settled at Casaseca de las Chanas in the province of Zamora and began to make wine in cellars dug into the limestone, naming the house Bodegas Porto after their home village. In the 1970s their son, by the house's account, brought the harvest forward and took the house's reds from 16 or 17 degrees of alcohol down to 13 or 14. In those years the family sold its first wines of Tinta de Toro under the name Colegiata, with a label drawn from the collegiate church of Toro, and, as the house tells it, the first Gran Colegiata went into a Burgundy shaped bottle, then a mark of quality. The family later moved its cellar into Toro, and when the Denominación de Origen Toro was recognised by an order of 29 May 1987, the son became the first president of its Consejo Regulador. Gran Colegiata Original returns to that first bottle's shape. For a sommelier it is the Toro of a family that bottled the town's red under its own label before the denomination existed.

others.note: Tinta de Toro from ungrafted vines over forty years old, aged twelve months in French oak barrels, by the house's page.

others.name: Colegiata
others.note: The house's younger range, a young, unoaked white of Malvasía among its wines, keeping the name under which the family first sold its Tinta de Toro.

traps: Gran Colegiata is named for Toro's collegiate church of Santa María la Mayor, not for a college or a vineyard.
Toro is the DO and Tinta de Toro the grape: Tempranillo under its local name, which must make up at least three quarters of a Toro red.
A Toro Reserva needs thirty six months of ageing with twelve in barrel; Gran Colegiata Original goes further, with eighteen months in American oak.

cards.front: Bodegas Fariña: where did the family begin in 1942, and under what name?
cards.back: At Casaseca de las Chanas, in cellars dug into limestone, as Bodegas Porto after the founders' home village.

cards.front: What do the words of Gran Colegiata Original's name recall?
cards.back: Toro's collegiate church of Santa María la Mayor, and the Burgundy shaped bottle of the first Gran Colegiata.

opts: The founders' son became the Consejo's first president
The family sold its cellar to a co-operative
The family left Toro for the new DO of Rueda

questions.exp: By the house's account and others, the founders' son became the first president of the Consejo Regulador of the DO Toro, recognised in 1987; Numanthia was founded only in 1998.

report: Searches for this record: 6 of the group's share of 35 (three on the house's own domain, one on the Consejo's, two wider); no fetch tried.

The plan's note is answered: 1942 at Casaseca de las Chanas rests on the house's history with Enterwine and Wine Tourism; the son's presidency of the first Consejo Regulador in 1987 on the house's history with Enterwine; the move into Toro is dated about 1970 in Vozpópuli alone (one other account has the son take over the cellar in 1965), so the story gives no year.

The bottling taught is Gran Colegiata Original, labelled Reserva on the house's page: the Colegiata name of the 1970s, the label drawn from the church and the first Gran Colegiata in a Burgundy bottle rest on the house's page with a merchant's listing (Vinissimus); the house's launch of the Original is a news item of its own, its first vintage not found.

The Reserva rule (thirty six months, twelve in barrel) and the three quarters of Tinta de Toro rest on the Consejo's own pages on its reds; the decree's date on the Consejo's copy of the order of 29 May 1987.
The church begun in the twelfth century rests on Turismo Castilla y León and Spain.info (1160 and about 1170 in two accounts, hence the century).

Left out: the founders' names and dates (none found), a blind tasting won by the 1982 Gran Colegiata in Switzerland (the house's account, and a ranking this tab refuses), and Fariña as one of three bodegas working when the DO began (one secondary account).

Living names met, none in the fragment: the founders' son, head of the house and first president of the Consejo, and his heirs; the founders are described, since no dates were found. No swap proposed.

changed: story and cards: a cellar dug into the limestone now cellars, three by the family's own telling, and naming the house Bodegas Porto.
story and label: the first Gran Colegiata's Burgundy shaped bottle hedged as the house's account (no source of the refuter's names it).

story, labels and question: the DO recognised, not created, by the order of 29 May 1987; the son became the first president of the Consejo Regulador (elected cut, since the order had the Ministry name the president), borne out beyond the house by Vivir el Vino and a trade profile.
story: the six bodegas that took up the seal cut (the house alone, against three in another account).
wine.glass: liquorice and the balsamic note cut; ripe blackberry and plum over cocoa, toast and vanilla, full bodied and poised, soft, silky tannin, on Guía Peñín for 2020 and Decanter for 2017.
others: Fariña Crianza's two years in bottle cut (no page read) and the house's page named; the Colegiata range a young, unoaked white of Malvasía, a red cut.

The year the family moved into Toro: 1987 in one importer's account and about 1970 in the author's; the change of name to Bodegas Fariña in 1986 in one merchant's account; none is in the record.
The Burgundy shaped bottle rests on the house's page and one merchant.
